investigative-questions-s1.title: Walking and blood pressure
investigative-questions-s1.html: A health researcher studied the medical records of 1,200 adults in a city. Adults whose records said they walked 30 minutes or more a day had a lower typical blood pressure than adults who walked less. The researcher did not ask anyone to change how much they walk (invented data).

investigative-questions-s2.title: Phones at lunch
investigative-questions-s2.html:
The student council at Lincoln High School, which has 1,500 students, wants to learn about phone use during lunch. Members suggest four questions:

  1. Do you like your phone?
  2. What proportion of Lincoln High students use a phone during lunch on a typical school day?
  3. Do phones cause students to eat less at lunch?
  4. How many minutes did Maria spend on her phone at lunch today?

items.q: What kind of study is this?

why.correct: The researcher observed walking and blood pressure without imposing any condition, so this is an observational study.
options: Comparing groups is not enough for an experiment; the researcher would have to decide who walks.
Right: the researcher recorded walking and blood pressure as they already were, without imposing anything.
1,200 adults are a part of the city, not every adult in it.
No one was asked anything; the data came from existing records.
An experiment
An observational study
A census
A sample survey, because the adults answered questions about walking

items.q: What are the explanatory and response variables?

why.correct: The explanatory variable is the one that may help explain changes in the response: walking explains blood pressure.
options: This reverses them. The researcher wants to see whether walking is related to blood pressure.
The city and the adults are the setting and the observational units, not variables.
Records are the data source, and a conclusion is not a variable.
Right: the question is whether walking helps explain blood pressure.
Explanatory: blood pressure. Response: daily walking time
Explanatory: the city. Response: the adults
Explanatory: medical records. Response: the researcher’s conclusion
Explanatory: daily walking. Response: blood pressure

items.q: Which is a possible confounding variable in this study?

why.correct: A confounding variable is linked to both the explanatory and the response variable, so their effects cannot be separated. Age is a strong candidate.
options: Right: a confounding variable is related to both the explanatory and the response variable, so its effect mixes with walking’s.
Blood pressure is the response variable itself.
The sample size is a fact about the study, not a variable recorded for each adult.
A confounding variable must be related to both walking and blood pressure; hair color is linked to neither.
Age: younger adults may walk more and have lower blood pressure
Blood pressure, since it is measured in each adult’s medical record
The number of adults whose records were studied, 1,200
Hair color, since it differs a lot from one adult to the next

items.q: Can the researcher conclude that walking more lowers blood pressure?

why.correct: Only a study that imposes the conditions, with chance deciding who gets which, supports cause and effect. Here the link may be due to confounding.
options: A large observational study still cannot rule out confounding variables.
A difference between groups that formed on their own can come from other differences between them.
Right: in an observational study the walkers may differ in other ways, such as age or diet, that affect blood pressure.
The measurement is fine; the problem is that walking was not imposed.
Yes: 1,200 adults is enough
Yes: the walkers had lower blood pressure, so walking caused it
No: it shows a link, and confounding may explain it
No: blood pressure is too hard to measure accurately to tell either way

items.q: Which is the best investigative question?

why.correct: A good investigative question names the population, the variable and the kind of answer (here a proportion), and can be answered with data that vary.
options: It is a survey item for one person, not a question about the population, and "like" is vague.
It asks about cause, which needs an experiment, and it does not name a population or a measurable variable.
Right: it names the population (Lincoln High students), the variable (phone use at lunch) and what to estimate (a proportion).
It has one answer about one student; there is no variation to study.
Question 1
Question 3
Question 2
Question 4

items.q: Question 2 asks about which kind of number?

why.correct: The question is about every student at Lincoln High, so it asks for a parameter, the population proportion.
options: Right: the question is about the whole school, so it asks for a population proportion.
The council may estimate the answer with a statistic, but the question itself is about the whole school.
The question asks about use at lunch, not ownership.
The question asks for a proportion of students, not minutes.
A parameter: the proportion of the whole school using a phone at lunch
A statistic: the proportion of the students who answer the council
A count of the phones that the students at Lincoln High own
A mean of the minutes that students spend on phones at lunch

why.correct: To estimate a proportion for a population, survey a sample chosen by chance from the whole population.
options: The council wants to know how students behave now, not the effect of a condition.
A census of 1,500 students’ phone records is impractical and private; a sample does the job.
Council members are not chosen to represent the school.
Right: asking a well chosen sample is practical and can estimate the school’s proportion.
An experiment in which some students are told to use phones
A census of each of the 1,500 students’ phone records from the past month
Asking the members of the student council what they do at lunch
A sample survey of students chosen at random from the school list

items.q: Why is Question 3 hard to answer with a survey?

why.correct: Questions about cause need an experiment. A survey or observational study shows only how variables are related.
options: Time is not the problem; the design of the study is.
Right: students who use phones may differ in other ways, so only an experiment that imposes phone use could show a cause.
They might answer; the issue is what the answers could show.
There is no such rule; the issue is cause and effect.
A survey of the students would take too long to finish
A survey can show a link, but a cause needs an experiment
Students would refuse to answer questions about their phones
Questions about food at lunch are not allowed in a survey

why.correct: A census gathers data from the entire population.
options: Right: a census measures the whole population, not a sample.
That describes an experiment.
That is a sample, and a poorly chosen one.
A census covers the whole population of interest, not one household.
A study that collects data on every member of the population
A study that imposes a condition on the people in the sample
A survey of a small group of people who volunteer to answer
A count of the people living in one house in a town

items.q: A teacher wants the typical number of hours her 28 students slept last night. Which is the most sensible plan?

why.correct: When the population is small and easy to reach, a census answers the question exactly.
options: A sample works, but with 28 students a census is easy and exact.
The teacher wants to know how long students slept, not the effect of a condition.
Right: the population is small, so measuring everyone is easy and gives the exact answer.
The question is about her own 28 students.
A sample of 5 students chosen at random from the class
An experiment
A census: ask all 28 students
A survey of students in another class at the school

items.q: Researchers enroll 5,000 adults who do not smoke, record their diets, and follow them for 20 years to see who develops heart disease. What kind of study is this?

why.correct: Prospective: follow individuals forward and record outcomes. Retrospective: look back at existing records. Both are observational when nothing is imposed.
options: Retrospective studies look back at past records; this one looks forward.
Right: it follows people forward in time, recording what happens, without imposing anything.
Length does not matter. No diet is imposed, so it is observational.
The 5,000 adults are a sample of nonsmokers.
A retrospective observational study of past heart disease
A prospective observational study
An experiment
A census of the nation’s adults who do not smoke and who eat a recorded diet

items.q: Which question can only be settled well by an experiment?

why.correct: A cause-and-effect question needs an experiment, in which the researcher imposes the conditions.
options: That describes a population; a sample survey answers it.
That is answered by measuring the plants as they are.
That asks about a relationship that already exists; an observational study answers it.
Right: a question about cause needs the researcher to impose the fertilizer on some plants and not others.
What proportion of a town’s gardeners grow tomatoes?
How tall are the tomato plants in a garden center today?
Do tomato growers grow peppers?
Does a new fertilizer make tomato plants taller?

items.q: What makes a study an experiment rather than an observational study?

why.correct: An experiment deliberately imposes conditions on individuals to measure their responses; an observational study does not.
options: Observational studies also measure many variables.
Right: in an experiment the researcher decides who gets which condition.
Experiments can happen anywhere; what matters is imposing conditions.
Size does not decide the type of study.
The researcher measures many variables at the same time
The researcher imposes a condition, then measures the response
The study is done in a laboratory, not out in the everyday world
The study uses a very large group of participants

items.q: Students who eat breakfast earn higher grades than students who do not. A news report says breakfast raises grades. What does confounding mean here?

why.correct: A confounding variable is related to both the explanatory and the response variables, so their effects on the response cannot be told apart.
options: Confounding is about variables mixing their effects, not about confusion.
That is a mixed effect, not confounding.
That is a concern about measurement, a different issue.
Right: if a third variable affects both, its effect is mixed up with breakfast’s.
The breakfast eaters were confused by the questions they were asked
Breakfast has mixed effects
The grades were recorded by the students themselves, not the school
A third variable, like family routine, may affect both

items.q: Which of these is an investigative question that data from a sample could help answer? Select all that apply.

why.correct: An investigative question names a population and a variable whose values vary, and asks for something data can estimate.
options: Right: it names a population and a variable that varies, and asks for a typical value.
One person, one answer: no variation to study.
A single fact to look up.
Too vague: no population, no measurable variable.
What is the typical commute time of employees at a company of 900 workers?
How long was my commute this morning?
What time does the company office open each day?
Is commuting bad?

items.q: A sample survey asks 400 adults whether they recycle. What kind of study is a sample survey?

why.correct: A sample survey is an observational study: it records answers from a sample without imposing anything.
options: Right: a survey asks people about themselves without imposing any condition.
Answering questions is not a condition imposed to see a response.
A census asks every member of the population.
A survey shows relationships, not causes.
An observational study that asks questions
An experiment, since the adults have to answer the questions
A census
A study that can show recycling causes changes in behavior
